preamble: Rounding of the open back vowel [ɑ] to the open back rounded [ɒ]. In Old English, short /ɑ/ was probably pronounced as rounded [ɒ] before nasal consonants. The evidence is orthographic: the same word is written with a or o, as mann or monn 'person'. Reconstructed pronunciations of Old English texts therefore write sang [ˈsɒŋɡ] 'song' and nama [ˈnɒ.mɑ] 'name' with [ɒ] in the stressed syllable, while unstressed /ɑ/ before a nasal stays [ɑ], as in hȳran [ˈhyː.rɑn] (Beowulf, line 10). In Middle English the short vowel merged with /æ/ as /a/.

languageExamples.context: Stressed short /ɑ/ before a nasal consonant

examples.note: Wiktionary lists song as an alternative spelling, and the word for 'person' is spelled both mann and monn.

From the reconstructed reading of the Lord's Prayer (Sīe þīn nama ġehālgod); the unstressed final vowel stays [ɑ]. Wiktionary's normalized transcriptions do not show the allophone (sang [sɑŋɡ], nama /ˈnɑ.mɑ/) and write the o-spelling with [ɔ] (monn /mɔnn/).
